note.text:
To solve a quadratic equation by factorisation:
1. Rearrange so that one side is 0: ax² + bx + c = 0.
2. Factorise the left side.
3. If a product is 0, one of the factors is 0: set each bracket equal to 0 and solve.
Example: x² − x − 12 = 0 → (x − 4)(x + 3) = 0 → x = 4 or x = −3.
Never divide both sides by x: in x² = 5x you would lose the root x = 0. Write x² − 5x = 0, x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 5.
A quadratic equation has at most two roots. Check each by substituting it back.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to solve any quadratic equation that factorises, including x² = kx, and reject roots that make no sense.
Builds on: Lessons {5} and {6} (factorising trinomials) and Form Three linear equations.
Leads to: completing the square and the quadratic formula, for equations that do not factorise.

sections.heading: Why a product of {0} helps
sections.text:
If two numbers multiply to give {0}, at least one of them must be {0}. So once a quadratic is written as a product of two brackets equal to {0}, each bracket gives a root.
Solve {quad(1, -1, -12)} = {0}:
• Factorise: {lin2(1, -4, 1, 3)} = {0}.
• Either x − {4} = {0}, so x = {4}; or x + {3} = {0}, so x = {-3}.
Check x = {4}: {16} − {4} − {12} = {0}. Correct.
The rule works only when one side is {0}: (x − {1})(x − {2}) = {6} does not mean x − {1} = {6}.

sections.heading: Rearrange first
sections.text:
Bring every term to one side before factorising.
• {quad(1, 0, 0)} + {mono(2, 'x')} = {15} becomes {quad(1, 2, -15)} = {0}, so {lin2(1, 5, 1, -3)} = {0}: x = {-5} or x = {3}.
• {quad(1, 0, 0)} = {mono(7, 'x')}: do not divide by x. Write {quad(1, -7, 0)} = {0}, x(x − {7}) = {0}, so x = {0} or x = {7}.
• {quad(2, -1, -3)} = {0}: {lin2(2, -3, 1, 1)} = {0}, so x = {frac(3, 2)} or x = {-1}.
In a word problem, reject a root that makes no sense, such as a negative length.

key_words.meaning: a value of x that makes the equation true
an equation with x² as the highest power, such as {quad(1, -1, -12)} = {0}

mistake.why: Dividing both sides by x throws away the root x = {0}. Factorise instead.

steps: Factorise: two numbers with product {p * q} and sum {-(p + q)} are {-p} and {-q}.
Either x − {p} = {0}, giving x = {p}, or x + {-q} = {0}, giving x = {q}.
Check x = {p}: {p}² − {p + q} × {p} + {br(p * q)} = {p * p - (p + q) * p + p * q}.

Make one side {0} and factorise before using that rule.

misconceptions.explain: Dividing both sides by x loses the root x = {0}. Factorise x({poly([1, 'x'], [-k, ''])}) = {0} instead.
x² = {mono(k, 'x')} is not x² = {k}. Bring {mono(k, 'x')} over and factorise.
x − {br(p)} = {0} gives x = {p}: the root has the opposite sign to the number in the bracket.
That is the smaller root. The larger is {max(p, q)}.
The factors are {lin2(1, -p, 1, -q)}. x − {br(p)} = {0} gives x = {p}, not {-p}.
{p * q} is the number term, not a root. Factorise and set each bracket to {0}.
A quadratic has two roots here: the other bracket gives x = {q}.

solution: Each bracket can be {0}: x = {p} or x = {q}.

questions.prompt: Solve {quad(r * t, r * u + s * t, s * u)} = {0}.

misconceptions.explain: Moving {s} to the other side changes its sign: {mono(r, 'x')} = {-s}.

solution: {mono(r, 'x')} + {br(s)} = {0} gives x = {frac(-s, r)}; {mono(t, 'x')} + {br(u)} = {0} gives x = {frac(-u, t)}.

questions.prompt: A rectangular garden in Bamenda is {d} m longer than it is wide. Its area is {w * (w + d)} m². Write an equation in x, the width in metres, and solve it. What is the width?

misconceptions.explain: {w + d} m is the length. The width is {d} m less: {w} m.
A length cannot be negative: reject x = {-(w + d)}.

solution: Factorise: {lin2(1, -w, 1, w + d)} = {0}, so x = {w} or x = {-(w + d)}.
A width cannot be negative, so the width is {answer} m.
